description: The right panel locates the 1,880 primary Lacuna 2023 fields. Blue, orange and red mark the v1 training, validation and historical test labels. The other panels account for exclusions and monthly satellite coverage.

The right panel locates the same 1,880 primary Lacuna 2023 fields under the v2 split labels. Blue denotes development folds 1–4 and red denotes the held-back fold 0. The left panels show which records and months are available.

The v1 Ridge models summarize ten reflectance bands or five vegetation indices over alternative season windows. Paired bars give RMSE on the same 1,504 Lacuna fields for training with Lacuna alone and with 2024 records added. Shorter bars indicate smaller errors.

Each bar gives held-out Lacuna RMSE for one v1 training strategy. Dots at right show its difference from a matched Lacuna-only reference, with paired 95% spatial-group bootstrap intervals. Values left of zero favor the model being compared.

The v1 panels decompose squared error into bias and variance, compare seasonal, monthly and Presto features, and show uncertainty in the effect of adding 2024 records. The lower-right panel tests how well the 2024 source can predict its own held-out yields.

Bars give v1 tree-model RMSE on 1,504 Lacuna fields using imagery alone or with 46, two or four weather features. Compare the bars within each training panel to see how weather changes error, and corresponding bars across panels to see how adding 2024 records changes it.

The left panel compares v1 held-out errors for imagery and weather models trained with and without 2024 records. The other panels average January–March rainfall percent of normal and temperature departures over the same 97 weather cells in each year.

The histogram counts Lacuna fields by measured maize yield in tonnes per hectare. Its dashed line shows the mean. The adjacent bars show the percentage of fields with all ten satellite bands available in each month.
Each dot locates a Lacuna 2023 field. Colors identify the five test folds. The left panel assigns nearby villages to folds, while the right panel holds together fields in the same provider region.

Each dot gives a monthly-input model’s held-out RMSE in t/ha, with a 95% spatial-group bootstrap interval. The panels hold out villages or regions, and the dashed line marks the training-mean baseline. Farther left means smaller error.

The left panels compare measured and predicted yield for the monthly-band models. Color counts fields in each hexagon. The right panels show prediction minus observation against predicted yield, with positive errors above the horizontal reference.
For four monthly feature sets, each curve plots inner-validation RMSE against Ridge regularization strength on a logarithmic axis. The orange dot marks the minimum selected for regional outer fold 0.

Dots compare the held-out RMSE of whole-season features for new villages and new regions. Horizontal lines give 95% spatial-group bootstrap intervals. The dashed reference gives the RMSE of predicting the training mean.

Each dot subtracts monthly-input RMSE from seasonal-summary RMSE for the same feature family and held-out fields. A value left of zero favors seasonal aggregation. The lines give paired 95% spatial-group bootstrap intervals.

For the v2 experiment, paired bars compare Lacuna-only and combined-source Ridge fits on the same 1,504 Lacuna fields. The two panels show ten bands and five vegetation indices. The December–March calendar mean uses the same window for both providers.
The green boundary is a surveyed Malawi field. Each orange circle is a proposed sampling area. Increasing its radius or shifting its center 30 m moves part of the circle across the surveyed boundary.

Each Malawi 2023 field supplies a main crop cut on the horizontal axis and its nested subcut on the vertical axis, both in t/ha. The red point marks the example field. Distance from the diagonal shows how far its two measurements differ.

The red point and black outline locate the same Malawi field. The following panels translate its outline to 10 m satellite pixels in a 640 m square. The last two compare all touched pixels with those whose centers lie inside.

One Sentinel-2 acquisition shows a Malawi field outlined in yellow. The left and right views use visible light at two scales. The center assigns near-infrared reflectance to red, highlighting vegetation.

All ten panels show the same outlined Malawi field on one date. Panel titles identify the Sentinel-2 band, wavelength and native resolution. The common color scale measures reflectance across the bands.

Columns show five accepted scenes for the same Malawi field, outlined in red. The top row displays visible-color images. The lower row uses the legend to distinguish vegetation, bare soil and other scene classes across the surrounding chip.

For the example Malawi field, each colored line gives median reflectance across wavelengths during one observed month. At right, NDVI follows that field through the growing season, with gaps where a monthly value is missing.
Rows are months and columns are model inputs for the example Malawi field. Color shows the input value and gray marks entries masked before encoding.

Each bar shows one component of the frozen Presto embedding for the example field. Bar height is the encoded feature value after token averaging and normalization. The full vector represents the field in subsequent models.
Dots place fields by longitude and latitude in Kenya, Malawi and Zimbabwe. Gray dots give the full cohorts. Larger colored dots mark fields chosen for the archived 48-field imagery pilot.
Each row is a pilot field and each column is a month. Colors distinguish clear observations, cloudy attempts, absent scenes, bright-blue flags and download errors across four cohorts.
The yellow outline follows a Malawi 2023 field through monthly Sentinel-2 scenes. Gray tiles identify unavailable or cloudy months. Blue bars count clear field pixels and the green line tracks NDVI.
A red cross marks one Kenya OAF 2019 field location on the accepted monthly images. Bars count clear field pixels and the green line tracks NDVI from the available acquisitions.
A red cross locates one Zimbabwe 2024 record across nine monthly images. This example has a recorded zero yield. Blue bars count clear field pixels and the green line gives NDVI.

A red cross locates one Lacuna 2022 observation on the available Sentinel-2 images. Gray tiles identify months without an accepted scene. The green NDVI line and clear-pixel bars use the available dates.
Each tile shows a pilot field in its greenest accepted scene and gives its recorded yield in t/ha. Yellow boundaries identify polygon observations and red crosses mark point observations.

Each row represents the same pilot field across three feature families. The bar at left gives measured yield. Blue and red cells show feature values below and above their column means after standardization.

The curve tracks training mean squared error over 100 fine-tuning epochs on the usable pilot fields. Yield was standardized before fitting. The logarithmic error axis makes changes late in training visible.

Ten panels show a 640 m square around the same Malawi field in the same satellite acquisition. The yellow line marks the field. Lighter grayscale values indicate stronger reflectance in the band named above each panel.

The first three images display individual red, green and blue bands of the Malawi field. The last two combine them into visible color and a near-infrared composite, where vegetation appears red. Yellow outlines mark the same field.

Wavelength runs from visible light to infrared. Green and brown curves summarize reflectance for pixels classified as vegetation and bare soil in the chosen scenes. The dashed black line is the example field’s median, and shaded strips mark the Sentinel-2 bands.

Each layer is a monthly satellite view of one Malawi field. Yellow traces its boundary. The red vertical line marks one pixel through time, and translucent gray layers identify months without a clear scene.

The left heatmap shows monthly median reflectance by band for one field, with gray rows marking gaps. At right, the red and near-infrared band values from that table are combined into an NDVI time series.

Green shades at left show pixel-level NDVI within a surveyed Malawi field. The center histogram gives the distribution for its interior pixels. At right a red square marks the single 10 m pixel used for a Kenya point observation.

In a Malawi satellite chip, the red square picks a 3 × 3 pixel filter. The response map lights up where other patches produce a large filter response. The mean response produces one illustrative MOSAIKS feature.

These schematic cubes illustrate three ways to use an image sequence. The red column follows one location through time, the blue plane samples a whole image at one time, and the orange panel represents an annual embedding layer.

Each line tracks monthly field NDVI for one observation in the archived pilot. Within each cohort, brighter colors mean higher measured yield relative to that cohort’s maximum. Missing monthly observations leave gaps in the curves.

The histogram counts Lacuna fields by measured maize yield in tonnes per hectare. Its dashed line shows the mean. The adjacent bars show the percentage of fields with all ten satellite bands available in each month.
Each dot locates a Lacuna 2023 field. Colors identify the five test folds. The left panel assigns nearby villages to folds, while the right panel holds together fields in the same provider region.

Each dot gives a monthly-input model’s held-out RMSE in t/ha, with a 95% spatial-group bootstrap interval. The panels hold out villages or regions, and the dashed line marks the training-mean baseline. Farther left means smaller error.

The left panels compare measured and predicted yield for the monthly-band models. Color counts fields in each hexagon. The right panels show prediction minus observation against predicted yield, with positive errors above the horizontal reference.
For four monthly feature sets, each curve plots inner-validation RMSE against Ridge regularization strength on a logarithmic axis. The orange dot marks the minimum selected for regional outer fold 0.

Dots compare the held-out RMSE of whole-season features for new villages and new regions. Horizontal lines give 95% spatial-group bootstrap intervals. The dashed reference gives the RMSE of predicting the training mean.

Each dot subtracts monthly-input RMSE from seasonal-summary RMSE for the same feature family and held-out fields. A value left of zero favors seasonal aggregation. The lines give paired 95% spatial-group bootstrap intervals.

Each point compares two area-normalized measurements from the same Malawi field. Horizontal position gives main-cut yield and vertical position gives nested-cut yield in t/ha. Points above the diagonal have a larger nested-cut estimate.
Blue dots locate the primary records in Malawi 2023, Kenya OAF, Lacuna and Zimbabwe 2024 using longitude and latitude. Each panel title gives its cohort and record count.

The left column places a white zoom window on a Malawi polygon and a Kenya point. In the enlargements, blue marks pixels with centers inside the field, orange marks edge-only pixels, and the white outline or cross is the provider geometry.

The lines show monthly median field NDVI among available primary observations for each cohort and harvest year. Months run from October through the following September so growing seasons can be read across calendar years.

Five columns follow a Malawi field from January to June 2023. Visible-color images appear above their scene-classification masks. The white boundary marks the field, and the legend identifies cloud shadow, vegetation, bare soil and other classes.

Grayscale panels show ten spectral bands around the same Malawi field, outlined in orange. Lighter shades represent higher reflectance on a common scale. Wavelength labels distinguish the visible, red-edge and infrared bands.

The first two panels show the same Malawi scene in visible color and near-infrared false color. Vegetation appears red in the second view. The wavelength plot at right compares vegetation, bare soil and the field median.
Blue shades show NDVI across the outlined Malawi field on 7 March 2023. The adjacent histogram summarizes 79 interior pixels. The black line marks their median NDVI of 0.63.
This field’s reflectance heatmap places months in rows and spectral bands in columns. Gray denotes months without clear imagery. The curve at right summarizes NDVI across the available months.

For Malawi, Kenya and Lacuna, each point is a field and each color a test fold. The upper row groups locations using 2 km spatial connections. The lower row shows the regional split defined for each cohort.

The diagram follows provider records and Sentinel-2 observations through label checks, monthly measurements, season summaries and the features used in modeling. Connecting lines identify the joins between the tables.
Each panel counts fields in half-tonne-per-hectare yield bins for one modeling cohort. The vertical line marks that cohort’s mean. Panel titles give the field count and the number of zero yields.

Each row combines a cohort and harvest year. Percentages and blue shading give the share with nonmissing satellite measurements for each calendar month. Blank cells fall outside the displayed season for that cohort.

The density curves compare measured yields for 1,504 Lacuna development fields and 4,330 imagery-eligible Zimbabwe 2024 records in v1. Normalizing each curve by its sample size makes their shapes comparable. The 2024 curve includes recorded zero yields.

The bars summarize January–March conditions across the same 97 NASA POWER cells in the 2023 and 2024 harvest seasons. The rainfall reference line marks 100% of normal and the temperature reference line marks a zero-degree departure.

Paired bars compare training and held-out RMSE for merged v1 tree models with imagery alone or with 46, two or four weather features. The separation between bars shows how much prediction error grows on held-out fields.

A synthetic field outline and point illustrate four pixel-selection rules. Teal cells show the pixels retained by a point, two polygon rules, and a 20 m circular proxy. Each panel reports the resulting count.

On this synthetic 10 m grid, the left panel marks cloud pixels, the middle adds a 60 m margin, and the right shows retained pixels. The orange square locates an observation rejected because the margin reaches it.

Each stacked bar starts with the observations that met the original four-month rule. Teal shows the percentage still meeting it after stricter quality screening, while orange shows the percentage that lost sufficient coverage.

Rows of known Malawi field boundaries were tested with different circular sampling radii and simulated location offsets. The left curves show the median percentage of the circle inside the field. The right curves show the median percentage of the field covered by that circle.
This archived workflow traces ground observations and imagery through the prediction pipeline to held-out scoring. The arrows show dependencies among processing steps.
This archived sketch traces how the satellite observations for a field form a feature vector and how its crop-cut measurement supplies the yield target.
This archived decision diagram shows how pilot performance against a location baseline and the gain from fine-tuning determined the planned next experiment.
The provider manual counts crop-cut records in narrow bins of measured yield (Mg/ha). Most measurements appear near the lower end, with a long tail extending beyond 10 Mg/ha.

The manual plots reported yield divided by 100 horizontally against the same unscaled yield vertically. The red dashed line marks equal axis values. Dividing the horizontal values by 100 concentrates the points near zero on that axis.

Each point compares measured yield and a random-forest training prediction from the provider manual. The dashed diagonal marks equality. Points below it show training records for which the model predicted a lower yield than the crop cut.
The provider manual plots measured test-set yield horizontally against its random-forest prediction vertically. Vertical distance from the dashed equality line gives each record’s prediction error.
Horizontal bars rank five multispectral bands by importance in the provider’s yield regression forest. The red reflectance band B4 has the largest bar, followed by the near-infrared band B8.

After the provider tunes its yield regression forest, the bars give the fitted importance for each spectral band. B4 remains the highest-ranked band, and the other four have more similar importance values.

The Lacuna provider’s random-forest example predicts yield across Zimbabwe from multispectral raster inputs. Dark purple through yellow denotes lower through higher model output on the published 0–6 scale. White lies outside the displayed raster footprint.
This histogram counts the four categorical codes used to train the provider’s crop-mask classifier. Class 1 is the most frequent. The manual stores these class labels in a column named yield.
Bars rank five multispectral bands by importance in the provider’s crop-mask classifier. B4 has the longest bar, though the displayed importances are close across all five bands.
The Lacuna provider’s classifier assigns a crop class to each pixel in this Zimbabwe map. Purple, orange and yellow encode the published class codes 1–4.

Dots locate villages in the Kasungu district sampling frame in Malawi. Dark green, light green and orange identify high, medium and low peak NDVI classes used for sample selection. The black outline marks the district.

The Malawi fieldwork diagram locates the nested 5 × 5 m and 10 × 10 m crop cuts using distances from a field’s southwest corner. Crosses flag rejected placements and the check marks the accepted placement.

On the v2 eligible training rows, the left bars compare model RMSE on the same Lacuna holdout fields. The right dots give RMSE differences from the corresponding Lacuna-only reference, with paired 95% spatial-group bootstrap intervals.

The v2 panels compare squared bias and centered error variance, predictions using different feature families, and paired changes in RMSE when 2024 records enter training. The final panel reports R² within the eligible 2024 source population.

The left panel compares v2 Lacuna-only and merged tree-model errors with imagery alone and with weather. The two right panels place the 2023 and 2024 harvests in context using January–March rainfall and temperature over the same 97 weather cells.

The two v2 panels compare imagery-only, full-weather and compact-weather tree models trained with Lacuna alone or with eligible 2024 observations. Shorter bars mean smaller RMSE on the same 1,504 evaluation fields.
For the single-field memorization check, the curves show mean squared error across epochs using evaluation mode and fitting mode. Both reach about 0.0036 (t/ha)² by epoch 13.

The two lines trace the encoder and prediction-head gradient norms during the single-field check. A positive encoder norm shows that the training signal reaches the satellite encoder during backpropagation.
The one point pairs the training field’s observed yield of 3.58 t/ha with its final Presto estimate of 3.52 t/ha. The dashed equality line shows the small underprediction.

The two-field check tracks fitting-mode and evaluation-mode mean squared error separately across 100 epochs. Their separation reflects the different batch-normalization statistics used in these modes.
Encoder and prediction-head gradient norms are plotted by epoch during the two-field training check. Both series show when updates carry gradient signal through the model.
The two points pair observed training yields of 3.58 and 4.30 t/ha with estimates of 3.49 and 4.23 t/ha. The diagonal gives exact agreement for this two-field memorization check.

The zero-regularization run compares training and validation mean squared error through 50 epochs. Validation error reaches its minimum at epoch 6 and finishes at 3.89 (t/ha)² while final training error is 1.04 (t/ha)².
Lines show encoder and prediction-head gradient norms at each epoch in the zero-regularization run. Their median norms are 7.1 and 3.3, respectively. Peaks mark larger recorded gradients.

For the zero-regularization run, colors separate 128 training fields and 64 validation fields. Each dot pairs measured and predicted yield. Validation estimates span -1.30 to 5.71 t/ha, and the diagonal marks exact agreement.

The light-regularization run compares training and validation mean squared error through 50 epochs. Validation error reaches its minimum at epoch 9 and finishes at 3.89 (t/ha)² while final training error is 1.11 (t/ha)².
Lines show encoder and prediction-head gradient norms at each epoch in the light-regularization run. Their median norms are 7.3 and 3.8, respectively. Peaks mark larger recorded gradients.

For the light-regularization run, colors separate 128 training fields and 64 validation fields. Each dot pairs measured and predicted yield. Validation estimates span -1.23 to 5.68 t/ha, and the diagonal marks exact agreement.

The medium-regularization run compares training and validation mean squared error through 50 epochs. Validation error reaches its minimum at epoch 14 and finishes at 3.57 (t/ha)² while final training error is 1.24 (t/ha)².
Lines show encoder and prediction-head gradient norms at each epoch in the medium-regularization run. Their median norms are 7.3 and 4.6, respectively. Peaks mark larger recorded gradients.

For the medium-regularization run, colors separate 128 training fields and 64 validation fields. Each dot pairs measured and predicted yield. Validation estimates span -0.64 to 5.48 t/ha, and the diagonal marks exact agreement.

The strong-regularization run compares training and validation mean squared error through 50 epochs. Validation error reaches its minimum at epoch 14 and finishes at 2.96 (t/ha)² while final training error is 1.58 (t/ha)².
Lines show encoder and prediction-head gradient norms at each epoch in the strong-regularization run. Their median norms are 8.7 and 6.7, respectively. Peaks mark larger recorded gradients.

For the strong-regularization run, colors separate 128 training fields and 64 validation fields. Each dot pairs measured and predicted yield. Validation estimates span 0.44 to 5.62 t/ha, and the diagonal marks exact agreement.
